t: Three Outputs of Truly Great Teachers
q: No living person has thought more about the word "great" than Jim Collins has in his long and focused career. If you're a teacher in search of surprising insights into both your career and your life, you could do a lot worse than picking up Collins' Good to Great.
For me as an individual teacher, superior results look like efficiently and intelligently producing as much growth in my students as I can, given my constraints.
Distinctive impact means that, were we to vanish tomorrow, there'd be a "gaping hole" that could not be easily filled by any other teacher. If we went away, would we be missed — and why?
Ours is a now-now–NOW culture; we want overnight successes and wild trajectories. But you can't be great, according to Collins, if you're a flash in the pan.

Time, inevitably, brings setbacks. It brings easy years and hard years; seasons of white-hot passion and seasons of ennui. Producing superior results and having distinctive impact in the ebb and flow of years and decades…that's what makes an educator truly great.

t: Teaching Team Members to Care About Customers and Clients
q: The key is to understand that caring, curiosity and genuine interest are siblings that can’t be separated.
Instead, good leaders ask for proof. And the proof is in what they know about specific customers and clients, not in what they are instructed to do.
They ask for the customer’s backstory, where they came from, where they have lived, and how they grew up in the world.
When team members can’t answer these and other questions that reflect an understanding of specific customers and clients, the point is loudly made.
Team members who are peppered with questions about their customers don’t even know that they are being taught.
In fact, it is almost impossible to be curious without an elevated sense of caring.

t: Decisions Against Consensus Can't Be Because You're Smarter Than Everyone Else
q: Sometimes leaders feel compelled to go against the wisdom of the group. Even when everyone is insisting on north, sometimes leaders believe they must head south.
Leaders who are convicted about an opposing view usually hold a value or principle higher than everyone else.
Leaders who discard the group view because they believe they know better or are smarter than the collective wisdom of the team almost always make a huge mistake.
Instead of heeding the advice or exploring options, the Field Director went against the consensus and selected not to sand the field and watered the turf just days before the game.
He chose not to listen to anyone else because he thought he was smarter and wiser than the collective wisdom of several centuries of experience represented by the team.
In the end, the leader may very well go against the group, but they do so knowing it is principle and not personal vanity that drives the decision.
x: Leaders occasionally must go against group consensus, and this can be the right call when grounded in values.

t: #58 Use the 4-2 Approach for Independent Work
q: Well, I have been experimenting with the 4-2 approach for the last few years.

Likewise, 2 minutes is enough for a focussed, productive discussion, but not long enough for those discussions to drift off-task.
If students are not used to working silently, those first 4 minutes will feel more like 4 hours, so feel free to adjust accordingly.

t: The Pain of Leaving Your Team for Another Opportunity
q: Good leaders feel a deep responsibility for the team they have helped to create.
When leaders choose to exit, their goal must be to depart as a “good leaver,” respecting the needs of the organization and team as much as their own.
Good leavers depart on good terms. Regardless of the official notice period, they commit the time to close the books on the past before moving on to the future.
They don’t apologize for leaving, but instead thank people for their contribution and support.
Good leavers, like good leaders, are in short supply. They shouldn’t be.
x: Leaving a team leaders helped build creates real, unavoidable tension between loyalty and opportunity.
There are no clean answers, only leaders who choose to depart well or poorly.
Good leavers commit real time to a transition plan, documentation, and successor prep before leaving.

t: Why You Must Say No To Pleading Students
q: Once you give in, even one time, you’ll open the floodgates and every planned activity will feel like a negotiation.
Anything less than novelty or surprise relief will be a crushing blow. This isn’t an exaggeration. No matter the age, give an inch and they’ll want a mile.
If you give in to please your students, you’ll send the message that the activity in question is inherently distasteful. It doesn’t have value or reward in and of itself.
The best way to respond to pleading is to immediately say no. Because once you pause, you’re in trouble.
Show your students that in the midst of struggle is where they’ll find beauty and the greatest joy.

t: Good Leaders Help Others to Recognize Harmful Patterns in Their Behavior
q: Patterns are hard to discern when they involve us. We can see patterns in others much easier than the consistent reactions and responses we employ.
The best leaders observe and collect our patterns and then debrief us to the possibility they are getting in our way.
Holding up a mirror for others and discussing patterns isn’t easy.
Leaders first make observations without evaluation (“When a colleague challenges you, your first reaction is to get quiet and withdraw from the conversation.”) and then stand ready to discuss them.
No one gets better without understanding the patterns that get in their way.
To paraphrase Mark Twain, harmful patterns and diapers must be changed for the same reason.

q: Leaders have been relying on a tree-like model to make decisions for decades.
By illuminating each choice or branch on the tree, the pivotal choices are considered one by one, thereby breaking down a highly complex decision into more manageable choices.
Not only does this visual transparency create more understanding and buy-in, but it is also a tool from which leaders can learn how better decisions are made.
The first step is to define the decision to be made and to identify all the possible alternatives or choices available.

t: Using AI as a Parent
q: As I've said in recent articles, I'm intentionally not good at most things related to teaching. To me, this is the key to being a good teacher while having a life.

Which is all to say, I'm not an expert on AI. It's effects on teaching, how to use it in the classroom, what it's doing to us and our students, where it will take education in the next five years…my answers to these questions are about as authoritative as any random teacher you'd ask.

It didn't just tell me the answer — I had the back of the textbook for that unhelpful bit of info. Instead, it gave me the full method for solving the problem. Once I read it, I knew how to help Haddie.

It can't make us care about others. I had to care about helping my daughter with homework to use the tool. And then I had to care way more to use the tool to help my daughter learn versus just using the tool to skip work.
It can't make us learn. Learning takes work — there's no away around it. You only remember what you think about, and if ChatGPT or its ilk do all the "thinking," well…you won't do the learning.

t: Leaders Who Own All of the Key Decisions
q: Some leaders can’t give up control or don’t feel comfortable unless they own all the important decisions for the team or organization.
In one well-known organization where the management team controls nearly every call, the senior team is known as “the deciders” by their colleagues throughout the enterprise.
The more team members succeed in their efforts to sway decisions they don’t like, the longer the line of people outside the leader’s door.
Instead, they clearly lay out what decisions they own and they push down decisions that are better made by others.
Leaders who refrain from influencing decisions they don’t own soon see the line of team members who need to speak with them disappear.

t: The Kiva Method for Inclusive Decision-Making
q: The tribal elders of the Hopi nation knew a thing or two about inclusive decision-making.
The so-called Kiva Method, drawn from the structures in which the decisions were made and devised generations ago, allows minor voices to influence more experienced views.
The most inner circle begins to debate and discuss the issue in question without any input from those in the two outer circles.
With each new discussion at the center, the outer rings only listen and learn, refraining from offering any input.
The power of this method revolves around its ability to create an inclusive discussion without having too many voices and viewpoints on the table at the same time.
By tapping into the collective wisdom of the organization’s leaders, perhaps no other method is equal to it.

t: When It Comes to End-Users and Customers, It's All About Reducing Friction
q: To achieve and sustain a competitive advantage in any marketplace, leaders must relentlessly reduce the friction end-users and customers experience with their products and services.
Friction refers to anything that makes it more difficult for end-users to realize the full value and benefit of a product or service.
Great organizations continually examine how end-users experience their product or service and identify every point of friction that exists.
Discovery friction includes any struggle about how to navigate or use the product or service.
Anything that chafes is a barrier to adoption and must be stamped out.
Eliminating friction is a never-ending job that pays big dividends in customer growth and loyalty.

t: At Some Point, You Have to Stop Repeating the Bad News
q: When things go horribly wrong, leaders face the difficult challenge of repairing a reputation and credibility that is now suspect.
Good leaders are patient in this process. They accept that people who were affected need to vent, be heard, and offer their views.
In every crisis or reputationally altering event, there comes a point where the bad news is keeping the bad news alive.
Even temporarily revisiting the crisis reopens the wounds and prevents real closure from happening.
Keeping the bad news permanently on the agenda is a losing strategy.

t: How to Speed Up Trust
q: Trust in relationships, on a team, and within an enterprise is the critical building block of effectiveness.
Trust built without a strong foundation of experience creates relationships that are fragile, superficial, and vulnerable to a single act which can erase it quickly.
If trust depends upon repeated interactions and experience with others, then leaders can purposefully expand the number of times such interactions occur in a given period of time.
In addition to more opportunities for interaction, those who want to accelerate trust often go out of their way to make small promises and to keep them religiously.
Keeping those promises exactly as they were offered deepens trust in a way nothing else can.
If others can’t count on you to take the small matters seriously, they know for certain you can’t be trusted on the large ones either.

t: Thinking Slowly About Loss Aversion
q: Nobel prize-winning behavioral economist Daniel Kahneman passed away at the age of 90 a few days ago.
Fast thinking is emotional, while slow thinking is analytical.
Kahneman found that people experience more psychological pain from losses than they do pleasure from equivalent gains.
This is why golfers make more putts for par than for birdie, why tennis players rarely miss the second serve, and why consumers are more likely to purchase unnecessary insurance and warranties.
Because of the loss aversion bias, people overestimate the probability of negative events happening.
Emphasizing opportunities, gains, and growth, as opposed to risks and potential loss, is a mindset good decision-makers develop on purpose.
